questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: What counts as a single stroke
questions.learningObjective: define a stroke in terms of pen movement rather than visual shape
questions.stem: A teacher defines a stroke as a line drawn in one continuous movement without lifting the pen, then asks how many strokes the character 门 mén, meaning gate, contains. Which count and which reason together answer the question correctly?

options.text: Six strokes, because the small hook at the end of a stroke is written with a separate flick of the wrist and therefore has to be counted on its own
options.misconception: treats the hook as a detached extra mark, when in writing the hook is the finishing movement of the stroke it belongs to

options.text: Three strokes, because each mark that turns a corner or ends in a hook is still a single continuous movement rather than two separate ones
One stroke, because the whole character can be written without lifting the pen if the writer is careful enough to keep the line going
options.misconception: confuses the possibility of an unbroken pen path with the recorded stroke count, which is a convention rather than a physical limit

options.text: Five strokes, because a visible corner where the pen changes direction must be counted as the end of one stroke and the start of another
options.misconception: counts every visible direction change as a separate stroke, which is the visual rather than the motor definition of a stroke

questions.explanation: The definition has to be about the hand, not the eye, and that single decision settles every counting dispute that follows. A stroke is one unbroken contact of the pen with the writing surface, and the pen may turn, bend or finish with a hook while that contact continues. The character 门 mén has three such contacts: a short stroke, a vertical stroke, and one stroke that comes down, turns along the bottom and finishes with an upward hook. A reader who counts what the eye sees gets a larger number, because the eye registers the corner and the hook as separate events. The eye is not wrong about what is on the page; it is answering a different question. The reason this matters beyond the single character is that stroke count is the second half of the standard lookup key in a Chinese dictionary, the first half being the radical, so a learner who miscounts strokes loses the character at the very point of trying to look it up. It also explains why the count for the same character can differ between two reference works without either being in error: two authorities can agree on what a stroke is and still write the components differently, which is the subject of a later item.
questions.hint: Ask whether the pen leaves the paper between the corner and the hook, and if it does not, how many contacts there were.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: The hook is not a separate stroke
questions.learningObjective: explain why a hook attached to a stroke is absorbed into that stroke
questions.stem: The character 子 zǐ, meaning child, is written in three strokes even though the page shows four distinct marks, because the first two strokes each end in a small upward hook. Why is the hook counted as part of the stroke it finishes?

options.text: Because the hook is produced by the same unbroken movement that draws the stroke, so it records where the hand stopped rather than a separate act of writing
Because a hook is only counted once per character, so a character with two hooked strokes would be recorded as having one fewer stroke than its visible marks
options.misconception: treats the rule as a quota on hooks rather than as a rule about which movements belong to which stroke

options.text: Because the hook is treated as a decoration added to a finished character, and decorations are not counted as writing at all
options.misconception: puts the hook outside the system of writing, when in fact it is part of how the stroke is terminated

options.text: Because hooks are only counted in formal printing and not in handwriting, so the handwritten form of the character has three strokes and the printed form has five
options.misconception: invents a difference between print and handwriting that the counting rule does not make

questions.explanation: A stroke count is a record of pen movements, so anything the hand does without breaking contact belongs to the movement in progress. When the writer reaches the bottom of a vertical in 子 zǐ and flicks the pen up, the pen has not touched down again; what the eye sees as a separate mark is the end of a single act. This is why the vocabulary of basic strokes is short: the strokes are named by the shape of the main body of the movement, and the two optional endings, a hook and a hook combined with a rise, are treated as properties of the stroke rather than as strokes in their own right. The practical test is therefore a question about contact, not about appearance. Ask whether the writing instrument left the surface. If it did not, one stroke; if it did, the next movement starts a new one. Applied to the same character, the test also blocks a common overcount: a character with several hooked strokes is not shorter by the number of hooks, and one with no hook is not shortened by anything. Keeping the contact definition straight is what lets a learner trust the number printed in a dictionary, which is the number they will need in order to find the character at all.
questions.hint: Ask what the pen is doing during the flick, and whether it is touching the paper while it flicks.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: A turning stroke counted once
questions.learningObjective: recognise that a stroke may change direction and still be one stroke
questions.stem: A student counts the character 九 jiǔ, meaning nine, as four strokes because the shape bends sharply in two places. What does the standard count of two strokes tell the student about where a bend may appear?

options.text: A bend may appear only in a vertical stroke, and a horizontal stroke that turns becomes a different stroke entirely
options.misconception: invents a restriction by direction that the counting rule does not make

options.text: A bend is allowed only when the character contains fewer than five strokes, since long characters are written more slowly and in smaller pieces
options.misconception: ties the counting rule to a length threshold, which has no basis in how strokes are defined

options.text: A bend may appear only at the end of a stroke, so a character that turns in the middle must be recorded as two separate strokes
options.misconception: restricts bends to stroke endings, which is the opposite of what the counting rule allows

options.text: A bend may appear anywhere inside a stroke, including a sharp turn at the bottom, provided the pen never leaves the surface of the paper

questions.explanation: The count of two for 九 jiǔ is the clearest available demonstration that position in space is not what makes a stroke. The character has a first stroke that begins as a falling movement, swings round into a horizontal, and finishes by hooking upwards, and that is one stroke because the pen travelled through all of it without touching down. Only the second stroke is a separate act. Since the shape of this one stroke includes a sharp corner, a corner cannot be the test, which disposes of the student's counting rule at a stroke. This is not a special dispensation granted to a familiar number; the same principle governs the long horizontal-and-vertical strokes of characters such as 门 mén and the compound enclosure shapes that appear inside many characters. The test remains the same in every case: contact with the surface, counted continuously, ending when the writer lifts or the movement stops by lifting. A learner who holds that test will find that many apparent overcounts disappear, and will also be able to explain the count of an unfamiliar character instead of guessing at it, which is what the following items build on.
questions.hint: Ask whether the direction of the pen changes while it is still touching the paper, and what would have to happen for a new stroke to begin.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: Adding the parts of a character
questions.learningObjective: compute the stroke count of a character from the counts of its parts
questions.stem: The character 四 sì, meaning four, is built from an enclosure of three strokes and a two-stroke part inside it. Given that a character's stroke count is the sum of the strokes in all of its parts, how many strokes does 四 have?

options.text: Three strokes, because a character is counted by its outermost shape and everything inside that shape is treated as decoration
options.misconception: ignores the inner component entirely, which is the error of counting only the frame

options.text: Six strokes, because the enclosure of three strokes is written with a separate closing stroke that the count has to add on top
options.misconception: adds a phantom stroke to the enclosure, confusing the visible outline with the number of pen movements

options.text: Four strokes, because the part inside the enclosure is joined to the enclosure and is therefore counted as part of one of its strokes
options.misconception: merges a separate component into a stroke of the enclosure, which would make the stroke count depend on how close the ink looks

options.text: Five strokes, which is the three strokes of the enclosure plus the two strokes of the part inside it

questions.explanation: Stroke count is additive over components, and 四 sì is a clean case to practise the addition on. The enclosure is written in three movements: a vertical on the left, a top stroke that turns down the right side, and a stroke that closes the bottom. The part inside is written in two movements, a falling stroke and a stroke that rises and turns. Three plus two is five, and that is the count that a dictionary prints and that a stroke index uses. The reason the additive rule is worth stating rather than assuming is that the alternative mental model, counting the outline, produces wrong answers in a regular way: it works for a character with nothing inside, and then fails for every character that has an interior part, which is most of them. The three distractors here are the three ways that failure shows up. One fuses the interior into the frame, one discards it, and one invents an extra stroke in the frame. Holding the two halves apart and adding them is slower for the first few characters a learner meets and much faster for the hundreds that follow, most of which are compounds of parts whose counts are already known.
questions.hint: Add the count of the outer component to the count of the inner one, and resist counting the outline as a single shape.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: Order of the parts inside a character
questions.learningObjective: state the order in which the parts of a character are read and written
questions.stem: The character 汁 zhī, meaning juice, is written as a three-stroke water component on the left and a two-stroke ten component on the right. In what order are the two parts read, and in what order are they written?

options.text: The left part is both read first and written first, because reading and writing both begin at the upper left of a character
The right part is read first and written first, because the component that carries the sound comes first in a compound character
options.misconception: makes the sound component prior in reading order, which is not what decides the order

options.text: Neither part has a fixed order, because the two components of a compound character can be read in either direction
options.misconception: assumes the order is free, when a fixed order is exactly what makes a character decomposable

options.text: The left part is read first but written last, because the reading goes across while the writing goes down the page
options.misconception: sends the writing in a different direction from the reading, which is not how character order works

questions.explanation: There is a single order that governs both reading and writing, and it can be stated in one sentence: work from the upper left. For a left-right compound such as 汁 zhī that means the left component is read first and written first, and then the right component. The rule extends to the other layouts in the obvious way, so a top-bottom character such as 花 huā is read and written from the top down, and an enclosing character such as 国 guó is read as the enclosure and then its contents, which is why a learner who learns the enclosure by finishing its outline will read the character in the wrong order. The order is not cosmetic, for two reasons. It is what allows a compound to be decomposed and looked up by component, and it is what makes the two parts of a sound-plus-meaning compound predictable, since the meaning component on the left narrows the field before the sound component is read. Learners who internalise the single rule of upper left therefore get the reading of a new compound approximately right even when they have never seen the character before.
questions.hint: Ask which side of the character carries the meaning, and then apply the one rule about where reading and writing begin.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: Two published counts for one character
questions.learningObjective: explain why the same character carries two stroke counts in different regional standards
questions.stem: One reference work counts the character 草 cǎo, meaning grass, as nine strokes, and another counts the same printed shape as ten. Where does the extra stroke come from, and what does that show about the two counts?

options.text: One work includes a stroke for the grass component's final flick and the other does not, so one of the two has made a plain counting error
options.misconception: assumes one authority simply miscounted, when the disagreement is systematic across hundreds of characters

options.text: The count differs because the two works were published in different centuries, and a count becomes correct only when every authority has adopted it
options.misconception: makes accuracy depend on unanimity, when a standard can be correct without being the only one in use

options.text: The grass component at the top is written with three strokes in the mainland standard shape and with four in the Taiwan standard shape, so the two works are counting two different written forms correctly
One work counts the traditional form of the character and the other counts the simplified form, so the difference disappears once the forms are written out
options.misconception: reads a difference in standard shapes as a difference between simplified and traditional, which is a separate axis entirely

questions.explanation: The difference sits in the shape of the component at the top. The mainland standard writes the grass component as a single joined horizontal crossed by two verticals, which is three pen movements, and 草 cǎo therefore totals nine. The Taiwan standard writes the same component as two separate crosses, which is four movements, and the same character totals ten. Nothing is wrong with either count, because the two authorities are recording the two shapes that their users actually write, and both shapes are correct within their own standard. The important conclusion is a negative one: the disagreement has nothing to do with simplified versus traditional characters. Simplified and traditional concerns which characters and which component forms are used, while this concerns the stroke breakdown of a single component that both sides use. The pattern is systematic rather than accidental, and it affects every character carrying that component, which is several hundred of them, so a learner who counts in one convention and looks up in the other will misplace characters across that whole class. The workable habit is to pick the convention of the material being studied and count by that convention throughout.
questions.hint: Count the top component of the character in the two ways it is written, and ask which standard each way belongs to.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: What a radical is
questions.learningObjective: define a radical as a lookup label rather than as a part with meaning
questions.stem: A dictionary arranges its entries under about two hundred headings, and a heading is a component that also often hints at the meaning of the characters filed under it. What is the dictionary's term for one of those headings?

options.text: A radical, which is the component a dictionary files a character under, whether or not it contributes anything to the meaning
A key, which is the position of a character in a list ordered by sound rather than by the components it contains
options.misconception: describes a phonetic ordering that is a different arrangement of the same entries

options.text: A phoneme, which is the smallest sound of the language and is used to file characters according to how they are pronounced
options.misconception: confuses the written classification of characters with the sound system, which dictionaries keep in separate sections

options.text: A morpheme, which is the smallest unit of meaning and is chosen because a radical always carries a share of the character's meaning
options.misconception: assumes a radical always contributes meaning, which fails for the many headings that are indexing devices

questions.explanation: The term is a radical, and the dictionary's use of it explains both the convention and the exceptions. A radical is the component under which a character is filed. The classical system of two hundred and fourteen radicals was a classification device, built so that every character in a large dictionary could be found without knowing how it was pronounced. The meaning connection is real and very often present, which is why so many radicals seem semantic: the water component appears in the characters for rivers, sea, lake and rain, and the speech component appears in the characters for talk, class and lesson. It is not universal, and the exceptions are what make the term worth defining carefully rather than by example. A character indexed under one component can have a meaning that has nothing to do with that component, which is the subject of a later item, and in simplified writing some radicals have short forms that a learner will meet before meeting the full form. What the radical is not is a sound. Two characters with the same reading can sit under different radicals, and two characters with the same radical can have different readings, because the sound is carried elsewhere in the character.
questions.hint: Ask what the heading under which a character is filed is called, and whether that heading has to carry the meaning.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: Size of the classical radical system
questions.learningObjective: recall the scale of the classical radical classification and what it was built for
questions.stem: The classical Chinese dictionary that gave the standard radical classification used a fixed number of headings, and the dictionary itself held close to forty-seven thousand characters. Roughly how many characters fell under each heading on average?

options.text: About two hundred and twenty, since dividing roughly forty-seven thousand by the two hundred and fourteen headings gives close to that figure
About twenty-two, since the same total divided by the headings gives a figure in the low twenties per heading
options.misconception: off by a factor of ten, the error of reading a total that is ten times smaller

options.text: About four hundred and forty, since a system with two hundred and fourteen headings averages twice that many characters per heading
options.misconception: doubles the quotient, which is the error of dividing by half the number of headings

options.text: About one hundred and ten, since the same total divided by the number of headings gives a figure just over one hundred
options.misconception: halves the quotient, which would follow from counting twice as many headings as there are

questions.explanation: The system was built at a scale that makes the average a useful thing to hold in mind. The dictionary of the Qing imperial compilation arranged its entries under two hundred and fourteen headings, a number that is fixed and that later dictionaries reused, and it carried close to forty-seven thousand characters. Dividing the total by the number of headings gives a quotient a little under two hundred and twenty characters per heading, which is the average. The average is worth knowing mainly because the distribution around it is wildly uneven, and that unevenness is the point. One heading, the grass component, was filed with close to two thousand characters, while one of the smallest headings held only a handful. So a learner should not picture two hundred and fourteen tidy boxes of equal size; the picture that helps is a few very large boxes, a great many middling ones, and a tail of tiny ones, with the most common characters more likely to sit in the crowded boxes. This is also why a dictionary asks for a radical as well as a stroke count: the radical narrows the search, and the stroke count orders what is left.
questions.hint: Divide the number of characters in the dictionary by the number of headings, and round the result.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: The uneven size of a radical classification
questions.learningObjective: infer the shape of a classification from its largest and smallest classes
questions.stem: In the classical radical classification, the grass component heads a section of close to two thousand characters, while one component heads a section of only five. What does that spread tell you about using the classification to find a character?

options.text: That the grass component is not a radical at all, because no genuine radical can head a section that large
options.misconception: concludes that a real classification has a size limit, when the grass section is a well known part of the system

options.text: That the headings are very uneven, so the radical narrows the search a great deal in a crowded section and hardly at all in a small one
That the small section must be a printing error, since five characters is too few to be a heading in a dictionary of that size
options.misconception: supposes the small figure is a mistake, when small sections are a normal feature of the system

options.text: That the headings are roughly equal in size and the two figures are outliers, so the radical always narrows the search by about the same amount
options.misconception: reads the two extremes as noise around a uniform distribution rather than as the distribution itself

questions.explanation: The classification is a picture of the language rather than an even grid, and the two figures are the clearest evidence of that. A section of close to two thousand characters under the grass component reflects how productive that component is: it goes into the names of plants, of dishes, of colours, of many everyday objects, and it combines freely with other components. A section of five reflects a component that is essentially finished as a productive element, usable in a handful of characters and then not again. The consequence for anyone searching is direct and is worth internalising. The radical is the first half of a lookup key, and how much it narrows the field depends entirely on which radical the character happens to be filed under. Under a crowded one it takes real work to finish, which is why dictionaries supplement it with a second key, the stroke count, and why modern lists also supply a table that orders characters by stroke count alone. A learner who expects the radical to do most of the work will be disappointed by the crowded sections and pleasantly surprised by the small ones, and in both cases the second key is what finishes the job.
questions.hint: Compare what a searcher still has to look through after choosing a crowded radical and after choosing a small one.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: Radicals that take a shorter form on the left
questions.learningObjective: recognise a radical that changes shape when it occupies a particular position
questions.stem: The speech radical appears as the full form 言 yán in 言 yán itself, and as a short two-stroke form 讠 on the left of a character such as 说 shuō, meaning to speak. What does the short form show about radicals and their position?

options.text: A radical is only ever written in one form, and the short form seen on the left is a simplified character with a different meaning
options.misconception: turns a positional variant into a separate simplified character, confusing two different systems

options.text: A radical may have a different written form when it stands on the left, and the short form is the same radical rather than a different one
A radical keeps its full form in every position, so a short form on the left indicates that the character has been written incorrectly
options.misconception: treats an ordinary positional variant as an error, when the short form is the standard form in that position

options.text: A radical changes into a different radical when it moves to the left, so the two forms belong to two separate sections of a dictionary
options.misconception: splits one radical into two, which would double the size of any classification built on headings

questions.explanation: A radical is a component identified by what it does in a character, not by a fixed picture, and the language exploits that freedom heavily. The speech component is written with its full shape when it stands alone or in a central or bottom position, and with a compressed shape when it is placed on the left, where the space is narrow and the strokes would otherwise collide with the rest of the character. The same pattern runs through the other frequent left-hand radicals, so the hand component, the food component, the silk component and the metal component all have short left-hand forms alongside their full forms. A practical consequence runs straight through to the simplified writing of the language. The short form of the speech component is one of a small set of short components that the simplification scheme adopted on purpose, because replacing a long component with a short one of the same sound cuts a great many characters at once. The thing to hold on to is that short form and full form are two writings of one radical, so a character indexed under one is indexed under the other in a dictionary that treats them as the same heading.
questions.hint: Ask whether the two shapes are one radical written twice or two radicals, and what decides which shape appears.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: A radical that keeps its shape everywhere
questions.learningObjective: identify an enclosing radical that does not vary with position
questions.stem: The enclosure component appears in 国 guó, meaning country, 园 yuán, meaning garden, and 图 tú, meaning diagram, and in each of those it is written as a full surrounding box of the same size. What makes this component unusual?

options.text: It keeps the same shape and the same size in every position, because it surrounds the other parts instead of sitting beside or above them
It is never used as a heading in a dictionary, because a component that appears in so many characters is too common to index
options.misconception: assumes a component's usefulness for indexing depends on being rare, when headings are chosen for productivity

options.text: It is the only radical that can never be written in a short form, since no compressed version of a surrounding box has ever been devised
options.misconception: states a uniqueness that the language does not support, since other radicals also resist compression

options.text: It is always read before the parts it surrounds, which is why the character takes its tone from the box rather than from its contents
options.misconception: claims the enclosure governs the reading, when tone and sound normally come from elsewhere in the character

questions.explanation: The rule behind radicals that take short forms is space. A left-hand radical is squeezed into a narrow column, and a bottom radical has to share its height with the part above it, so both are written in compressed shapes to fit. An enclosing radical has a different problem, and a different solution. Because it has to hold the other parts inside it, it is written at full size in every character it appears in, and the enclosed part is drawn to fit the space that is left rather than the other way round. That is why the boxes in 国 guó, 园 yuán and 图 tú are all the same size, and why the components inside them vary: the box does not compress, the contents do. The contrast is instructive when set against the left-hand radicals, which do the opposite and shrink. Recognising which behaviour a radical shows tells a learner something practical about the shape of an unfamiliar character before knowing anything about its meaning, because it predicts whether a component will look reduced or full size, and therefore whether the character is being written in a conventional way or has simply been crowded.
questions.hint: Ask why a left-hand radical shrinks and whether the same pressure applies to a component that has to surround the others.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: When the indexing radical is not the meaningful one
questions.learningObjective: recognise that a character's index radical need not carry its meaning
questions.stem: The character 桌 zhuō, meaning table, is filed by a dictionary under the wood component, even though the thing described is a piece of furniture and not a tree. What does that filing tell a reader about the relationship between a heading and a meaning?

options.text: The heading is wrong, and a dictionary that files this character under wood rather than under furniture is in error
options.misconception: treats a long-settled convention as a mistake simply because it is not obvious from the meaning

options.text: The heading is a filing decision that the language settled early, and a character can carry on without any relation between the two afterwards
The heading changes with the meaning, so the same character is filed differently in different dictionaries and no single answer exists
options.misconception: infers instability where the convention is actually stable across the dictionaries that use it

options.text: The heading guarantees the meaning, so a character filed under wood must refer to wood or to something made from it
options.misconception: takes a filing convention as a semantic guarantee, which is the assumption the exception exists to break

questions.explanation: A heading records where a character was filed, and where it was filed is a historical fact that later drift can detach from the meaning. Many characters began life as a combination in which the component now used as the heading really did contribute to the sense, and then the sense moved, usually because the sound of the character drifted towards something that had little to do with wood. The result is a filing convention that has to be learned alongside the character rather than inferred from it. This matters for two practical reasons. The first is that a learner who expects the heading to explain the meaning will confidently mis-remember the character, storing a false connection that resurfaces as a wrong guess later. The second is that it explains the pairs that make the system teachable. Where the same sound component appears with two different headings, as it does in 蜂 fēng, a bee, and 峰 fēng, a mountain peak, the heading is what tells the two meanings apart, and in those cases the heading is semantic. The rule that fits all the cases is that the heading is usually a reliable hint and is never a guarantee.
questions.hint: Decide whether the component a character is filed under has to contribute to its meaning, and use a pair of same-sound characters to test your answer.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: Single-part against multi-part characters
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a character built in one piece from one assembled from parts
questions.stem: The character 人 rén, meaning person, cannot be taken apart into two smaller meaningful parts, while 明 míng, meaning bright, can be taken apart into a sun component and a moon component. Why is the first kind harder to look up?

options.text: A character that cannot be decomposed is always rarer than a compound one, so the difficulty comes from how seldom it appears in texts
options.misconception: ties the lookup difficulty to frequency, when 人 is among the most frequent characters in the language

options.text: A character that cannot be decomposed has no component to search under, so a dictionary has to file it under its own shape as a heading
A character that cannot be decomposed cannot carry a tone, so the reading of such a character has to be supplied by the reader's ear
options.misconception: suggests tone depends on decomposability, when every character carries a tone either way

options.text: A character that cannot be decomposed is excluded from dictionaries, because the headings of a dictionary must be components rather than whole characters
options.misconception: reminds the reader of a rule that dictionaries break whenever they file a simple character

questions.explanation: A radical classification is a claim that most characters can be filed under a component, and the characters that cannot be decomposed are the residue that the claim has to absorb. 人 rén is one of them, and there are not many such characters, but they include some of the highest-frequency items in the language, so the residue is not a set of curiosities. A dictionary handles them by letting a whole character serve as its own heading, so a reader looking for 人 searches for the shape itself and then counts strokes to narrow the field. This is exactly why the second half of the lookup key exists, and why modern lists of characters also arrange material by stroke count alone: the simple characters are the ones that the radical step cannot help with, so a second key is not a convenience but a necessity. There is a practical lesson here for a learner as well as a searcher. When a character does not come apart, a mnemonic based on its parts is unavailable, and the character has to be learned as a shape together with a reading and a meaning. Recognising which category a new character falls into tells the learner in advance whether to look for a story behind it.
questions.hint: Ask what a dictionary uses as the heading for a character that has no component, and why the stroke count then matters more.

questions.topic: Two characters built from the same sound component
questions.learningObjective: use a shared sound component and the differing radical to separate two same-sounding characters
questions.stem: The character 蜂 fēng, meaning bee, and the character 峰 fēng, meaning mountain peak, share the same right-hand component and are pronounced alike, but they are filed under different headings. Which component decides the difference in meaning?

options.text: The right-hand component decides it, since the two characters differ only in what surrounds that shared part and share it entirely
options.misconception: assigns the difference to the component the two characters actually have in common

options.text: The tone decides it, since two characters pronounced the same way can only be told apart by a difference of tone
options.misconception: invents a tonal difference between two characters the question states are pronounced alike

options.text: The stroke count decides it, since a dictionary orders same-sounding characters by how many strokes each one has

The shared component on the right carries the sound, and it does that well enough that the two characters are pronounced alike and stay alike. The heading on the left carries the meaning class, and it does that by pointing at a domain: the insect component is found in the characters for bees, wasps and hornets, the mountain component in the characters for peaks and summits. This division of labour is why so much of the written vocabulary can be handled by a learner who has met only a few hundred components. Meet the mountain component once and every character built on it that appears in a text has a first approximation to its meaning, which is often enough to pick the right word before any dictionary is opened. The two claims also have different reliability, and the difference is worth holding on to. The sound component is a good but imperfect guide to the reading, because its own reading has drifted over centuries and no longer matches. The heading is the better guide to the meaning, for the reasons given in an earlier item.

questions.topic: What a sound-and-meaning compound lets you predict
questions.learningObjective: predict the reading of an unseen compound from its sound component

options.misconception: promises a perfect prediction, when sound components have drifted and only approach the target

options.text: Almost nothing, because the reading of a character is fixed by convention and cannot be inferred from any of its parts
options.misconception: assumes a reading is unreachable from the shape, which is what makes the sound component worth learning

options.text: A great deal, because the right-hand component supplies an approximate reading, while the left-hand component suggests the field of meaning the character belongs to
Nothing at all, because only the left-hand component is a real component and the right-hand part is an unrelated decoration
options.misconception: dismisses the sound component, which is a productive element in most of the language's compound characters

questions.explanation: The structure that makes a compound predictable is the sound-and-meaning compound, and it covers a large share of the characters a reader meets in ordinary text. Its logic is a division of labour between the two parts. The component on one side names the domain of meaning, which is why the water component appears in so many characters about liquids and about washing and clearing. The component on the other side was borrowed for its sound and contributes an approximation of the reading. The word approximation matters, and it is the part that a learner tends to overrate. Sound components have drifted over the centuries, sometimes by a small amount and sometimes by a great deal, so the prediction narrows the field of possible readings without fixing the answer. What the structure does buy is real: a reader who knows that the four-part component is read somewhere near qing can usually produce a plausible reading of an unfamiliar character, which is enough to look the character up or to follow a passage, and that is far better than having no reading to try. The meaning side is the steadier of the two, and the pair of characters discussed earlier shows why.

questions.stem: The character 林 lín, meaning grove, writes the wood component twice, and the character 森 sēn, meaning dense forest, writes it three times. What does the number of copies contribute to the meaning?

Repetition shortens the character, since each extra copy is written with fewer strokes than the first one
options.misconception: invents a stroke economy, when every copy in these characters is written in full

options.text: Repetition changes the tone, because the number of copies is one of the things that determines how a character is pronounced
options.misconception: attributes a tonal function to repetition, which is not a tone cue in this language

options.text: Repetition is only decorative, and the number of copies carries no information beyond making the character fill its square
options.misconception: dismisses a regular and productive pattern as mere decoration

questions.explanation: Writing a component more than once inside one character is a productive way of building an intensifier, and the pattern is visible well beyond the wood example. The character for three mouths stacked, 品 pǐn, is not three mouths in isolation but a graded notion of small things, of goods, of an article. The character for three suns, 晶 jīng, is not three suns but the quality that repeated brightness gives, sparkle and lustre. In each case the copies are counted and the count is doing the semantic work, in the same way that an intensifier works in a spoken language. Three points follow for a learner. First, repetition of this kind is one of the commonest ways a new character is built, so recognising it is a real shortcut. Second, the copies are written at full size, not abbreviated, which is the opposite of the compression seen in left-hand radicals and is a reminder that components behave differently depending on the job they are doing. Third, the resulting meanings are graded rather than plural, so the character names a degree or a collection and not a count of separate objects, and that distinction is what keeps a reader from translating the character as a simple number.

It lets a database store the character more compactly, since a code takes up less space than the character itself
options.misconception: gives a storage benefit as the reason, when the real gain is the ability to search structurally

options.text: It records the order in which the strokes are written, so a typing system can reproduce the character stroke by stroke
options.misconception: confuses a layout record with a stroke-order record, which is a different piece of data

options.text: It records the meaning of the components, so a translation system can read the character without a dictionary

A user who knows a character contains the water component and the character for green can ask for every character built that way and get a list, which is exactly how one studies productive components and how one finds the rarer members of a family. The same record supports sorting, so characters can be grouped by layout rather than only by code point, and it supports input methods, which can offer a candidate built the way the user has already begun. Three limits are worth stating so the code is not over-read. It records layout, not stroke order, so it cannot tell a typist how to move the pen. It records components, not meanings, so it cannot translate. And the decomposition it records is a scholarly judgement, so a database can disagree with another database about the same character without either being wrong. Read with those limits, the code is a description of a character's bones, and a useful one precisely because it is separate from everything else a character carries.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: The five named script styles
questions.learningObjective: name the recognised script styles and what each was used for
questions.stem: Chinese writing has conventionally been discussed in five named styles that range from a formal book hand to a highly abbreviated one. Which sequence runs from the most formal and slow to the fastest and most abbreviated?

options.text: Cursive script, running script, regular script, clerical script, then seal script
options.misconception: reads the sequence backwards, turning the fastest and most abbreviated style into the most formal

options.text: Seal script, running script, clerical script, cursive script, then regular script
options.misconception: puts the two joining styles in the wrong order and moves the standard book hand to the end

options.text: Seal script, clerical script, regular script, running script, then cursive script
Clerical script, seal script, regular script, cursive script, then running script
options.misconception: swaps the two oldest styles and reverses the last pair, so no part of the sequence is in order

questions.explanation: The five names describe degrees of formality and speed, and the order runs from the most ceremonious to the most hurried. Seal script is the old formal hand of inscriptions and seals, with rounded even strokes and fixed proportions, and it survives mainly as a name for the script of bronze and early stone inscriptions. Clerical script is the next stage, and it is the one with the practical history, since its flatter, squarer shapes were easier to write quickly on bamboo slips and then on paper and therefore became the script of clerks and eventually of printing. Regular script is the fully settled book hand, one stroke at a time, with every character the same size on the same square. Running script joins neighbouring characters and drops strokes, and cursive script abbreviates far more aggressively and is genuinely hard to read without training. The sequence is not simply a matter of taste, and the middle two entries are doing the work in the story: clerical script is what made writing an administrative technology, while running and cursive are what made it usable at speed once the clerical form had made the written page affordable.
questions.hint: Ask which style was the slow formal book hand and which two styles exist to save time, then put them in order.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: Why clerical script suited administration
questions.learningObjective: explain the connection between a script's shape and the speed of writing it
questions.stem: Clerical script became the working hand of clerks and officials for a very long period. What is the connection between the shape of that script and the work it was used for?

options.text: Its shapes were designed so that only trained clerks could read them, which kept official records out of ordinary hands
options.misconception: invents a script-based access restriction, when the script was deliberately easier to use

options.text: It was the only script that could be carved into stone, so administration followed from the material rather than from the shape
options.misconception: ties the script's administrative role to carving, which is a claim about stone rather than about the hand

options.text: Its characters were ornate and difficult, which made them hard to copy and therefore a reliable way to stop clerks inventing records
options.misconception: claims difficulty was an administrative virtue, when the point of the reform was the opposite

options.text: Its strokes were flattened and simplified enough to write quickly on slips and paper, which made routine written records practical at scale

questions.explanation: The shape follows from the medium, and the medium is the reason the style mattered. The earliest formal hands were written on materials that demanded care, because a slip of bamboo or a strip of wood is unforgiving and a wide, sweeping stroke needs space that the surface may not have. Clerical script answered that constraint by flattening the tall proportions of the earlier forms into a squarer shape, by converting curves into straighter segments and by breaking some joined movements into separate ones. Those changes reduced the number of movements the hand had to make and the precision each one demanded, and the result was a script that could be produced in quantity. Once that was true, everything downstream followed. Routine documents, registers, accounts and letters became cheap, and an administration that keeps written records is a fundamentally different kind of state from one that relies on memory and on messengers. The style later hardened into regular script for formal writing, but the connection between writing that can be produced fast and institutions that depend on written records is the substance of the story.
questions.hint: Ask what the earlier formal script was like to write on bamboo and paper, and what clerical script changed about that.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: Regular script as the printed standard
questions.learningObjective: explain why one script style became the model for printing and handwriting
questions.stem: Printed type in Chinese for centuries was modelled on the fully written-out, stroke-by-stroke book hand rather than on the two quicker joining styles. What did that choice buy for readers?

options.text: A settled shape for every character that could be recognised and referred to, which is what allowed dictionaries and printed texts to agree with each other
A denser page, because the joining styles leave more white space between characters than a fully written-out hand does
options.misconception: reverses the density relationship, since a settled hand leaves more room than an abbreviated one

options.text: A faster press run, because the fully written-out shapes have fewer separate pieces of type to be cast and assembled
options.misconception: claims a mechanical advantage, when the number of type pieces follows from complexity rather than speed

options.text: A way to write quickly by hand, since a printed page taught readers the standard shape and the standard shape was easy to write
options.misconception: reverses the direction of influence, when printing followed the hand rather than leading it

questions.explanation: A printed page is a reference object, and that is what made the choice of model matter so much. The fully written-out hand has one identifiable shape for each character, written the same way by every competent writer, which is precisely the property a printed text needs: a reader in one province and a reader in another must be looking at the same graph and finding the same character. The two quicker styles do not have that property on their own, since their abbreviations and joins vary with the writer and with the speed of the moment, which is why a text set in a joining style is hard to read even for a reader who writes that style fluently. Regular script therefore became the reference form that dictionaries described, that schoolbooks taught, and that type reproduced. One qualification is worth adding, because the simplified distinction is convenient and slightly wrong. The typefaces themselves developed features of their own, most obviously the flared stroke endings of the print styles, so that a printed character is recognisably not quite a handwritten one. The model is regular script and the product is a relative of it, and understanding that keeps the relationship clear.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader needs a printed character to be in order for two readers in different places to agree about it.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: Simplification by replacing a component
questions.learningObjective: identify the component substitution that produced most simplified forms
questions.stem: The simplified writing of the language replaced a long component with a short one of the same sound in a very large group of characters. What made that particular change so productive?

options.text: One substitution could be applied again and again, so a short component used once simplified a whole family of characters at the same time
It made the characters easier to pronounce, since a shorter component is read more quickly by a speaker of the language
options.misconception: confuses a written change with a change in speech, which the reform explicitly left alone

options.text: It removed the need for tones, because a short component could not be confused between two different tones
options.misconception: claims an effect on tone, which no change of component shape had

options.text: It gave each simplified character a new meaning, so that a reader had to learn the meanings again from scratch after the change
options.misconception: describes the change as semantic, when it was a change of written shape only

questions.explanation: The scale of the reform is explained by the fact that it worked on components rather than on characters one at a time. The scheme did not propose a new shape for every character separately; it proposed a small number of short components and then allowed those to be substituted wherever the long component had stood. The speech component is the standard example, and the rule was stated explicitly in the official instructions: a character containing the shortened form is simplified in the same way, whether or not that particular character happens to be listed. That is why a list of a few hundred listed forms implies a much larger set of actual forms, and why the authorities who drew up the tables had to add a third table of forms derived in exactly this way. The other two candidate explanations are attractive precisely because they are wrong in an instructive way. Nothing about the substitution changed a reading, since the point was to keep the same sound, and nothing changed a meaning. What changed was the number of movements the hand had to make, and the number of learners who could be expected to master writing at all.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to every other character that contains the component being replaced, and count how much work that saves.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: A simplified form that was already a character
questions.learningObjective: explain the difficulty caused by reusing an existing character as a simplified form
questions.stem: The simplified form used for the traditional character 後 is a character that already existed with an unrelated meaning of its own. Why does that reuse cause more trouble than a component substitution does?

options.text: The two traditional characters end up with the same reading, so a speaker can no longer say them differently in speech
options.misconception: claims a change in speech, when the readings of the two original characters were and remain distinct

options.text: The existing character had to be abolished, since a writing system cannot hold two characters at once in the same form
options.misconception: assumes a form can only belong to one character, which is the whole content of the difficulty

options.text: The two traditional characters now share one written form, so a reader meeting the form has to infer from context which of two meanings is meant
The character had to be given a new reading, because a form cannot be pronounced in two ways in the same language
options.misconception: invents a pronunciation limit, when one written form routinely serves several readings

questions.explanation: Reusing a form that already had a life of its own trades a writing problem for a reading problem, and the two are not equally serious. A component substitution leaves the character distinct: whatever the shape of the part, the whole is still one character, so a reader who knows the form knows which character is meant. When the simplified form is an existing character, two characters that meant different things and were written differently now share one shape, and the shape itself no longer says which is meant. The reader has to bring context to the task, and the number of contexts in which the decision is easy is much smaller than one would like. This is why the official comparison of standard characters with traditional and variant forms has to set out separately those cases where the correspondence is not one to one, and why a program that converts text automatically can go badly wrong on them, converting every occurrence of one form when only some of them should have changed. A converter needs a dictionary of exceptions; there is no rule that recovers the distinction from the shape alone.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader can and cannot tell from the single written form when two characters of different meanings share it.

questions.topic: Two traditional characters with one simplified form
questions.learningObjective: identify a simplified form that stands for two traditional characters
questions.stem: The simplified form 尽 stands for two different traditional characters, one meaning to the fullest and one meaning as much as one can. What does a one-form-for-two-characters mapping make impossible?

options.text: Reading the simplified form at all, since a form standing for two characters cannot be attached to any meaning
options.misconception: overstates the problem, since context does resolve the ambiguity in almost every case

options.text: Writing the simplified form, since a form that represents two characters has no single stroke sequence to follow
options.misconception: assumes the writing depends on which traditional character is meant, which it does not

options.text: Translating the two traditional characters, since a single simplified form can only be assigned one English equivalent

options.text: Recovering the traditional form from the simplified one, since the same simplified form corresponds to more than one traditional character

questions.explanation: The simplification of the language is not a one-to-one substitution, and the cases where it is not are what create the most practical difficulty. Where a long component was replaced by a short one, the traditional form can be reconstructed by putting the long component back, and the tables could therefore list a modest number of patterns and derive the rest. Where one simplified form stands for two traditional characters of different meanings, that derivation is simply not available. A machine converting in the other direction, which is what anyone reading an older text or working across the strait needs, cannot decide from the simplified form which traditional character to produce, and a human reader faces the same problem in a milder form. The number of such cases was eventually measured and published rather than left vague, and the official tables that accompany the modern standard list set them out, including the example of a form that corresponds to two traditional characters with different readings as well as different meanings. The practical lesson is that simplified and traditional text are related by a dictionary, not by a formula.

questions.topic: Adding up the simplified character table
questions.learningObjective: compute the total number of listed simplified characters from its three tables
questions.stem: The consolidated table of simplified characters is arranged in three parts, listing three hundred and fifty forms that cannot be used as components, one hundred and thirty-two that can, and one thousand seven hundred and fifty-three derived from those. How many simplified characters do the three lists contain together?

options.text: One thousand nine hundred and fifty-three, which results from adding the two smaller figures to the largest and dropping the middle one
options.misconception: drops a term from the sum, leaving a total that cannot equal the sum of the parts

options.text: Two thousand two hundred and thirty-five, since three hundred and fifty added to one hundred and thirty-two is four hundred and eighty-two, and that added to one thousand seven hundred and fifty-three is the total
Two thousand two hundred and thirty-six, which results from adding the three figures without regrouping any of them
options.misconception: a carrying error of one, the kind that comes from adding the hundreds before the tens

options.text: Two thousand two hundred and fifteen, which results from subtracting the smallest figure from the sum of the other two
options.misconception: subtracts a term that has no business being subtracted

The first list holds forms that may not be used as components, which is the rule that prevents a long component from being shortened in a character where the shortening would create a different word. The second list holds forms that may be used as components, together with a small set of short components that may be used on their own. The third list holds the forms derived by applying the second list across the language, and it is the largest because derivation produces far more forms than any list could print. Adding the three gives two thousand two hundred and thirty-five listed simplified characters, and that total excludes both the short components and the items in an appendix of forms that had long been treated as simplified without being listed. So the figure is the size of the three lists and not the whole of what simplification did, which is the distinction a reader has to keep in mind before quoting the number as a proportion of the language's everyday characters.

questions.topic: The three tiers of the modern standard list
questions.learningObjective: add the three tiers of the standard character list and state what each tier is for

The second tier, at three thousand, is the next band of general usefulness, and the two together form the six thousand five hundred characters that serve ordinary publishing, dictionary-making and information processing. The third tier, at one thousand six hundred and five, holds characters that are general within a specialised field, such as surnames, place names, technical terms and the classical characters that still turn up in school texts. The total is eight thousand one hundred and five, and the split matters more than the total for anyone deciding what a reader can be assumed to know. A list that simply said eight thousand characters would give no guidance about which characters could be assumed, which is the practical question for anyone setting text, building a reader's vocabulary or teaching.

The reason it is not lower is that component substitution multiplies: one short component on the list of replacements affects every character that contains it. The general lesson is that a mapping between two writing systems has to be treated as data to be checked rather than as a rule to be trusted.

The mainland list approves a simplified form for several thousand characters; the other side's approved forms are the traditional ones, and in a handful of cases the two sides do not merely differ over a simplified form but over which form should count as the standard shape at all. Two practical consequences follow. A reader crossing between the two traditions meets unfamiliar shapes, which is a real obstacle but a much smaller one than meeting a different script, since the component count, the component meanings and the sounds are largely intact. questions.stem: Some characters have always been written in two or more shapes that mean the same thing, and an official list of variant forms declared one shape standard and the others non-standard. How does such a case differ from simplification?

options.text: A variant form always belonged to a different character, which is why the list had to declare one of them standard
options.misconception: claims a difference of character, where the whole point is that the two shapes are the same character

options.text: A variant form was a character with a different reading, so the list had to choose which reading to allow
options.misconception: confuses two shapes with two readings, which are separate properties of a character

options.text: The variant list introduced the second shape, whereas simplification only ever removed shapes that were in use
options.misconception: reverses the direction of both processes, treating a list as an invention in each case

options.text: Both shapes were already in use for the same character, whereas simplification replaced one shape of a character with a new and shorter shape

questions.explanation: Two processes in the language's standardisation look similar from a distance and are in fact unrelated. A variant form is a second way of writing a character that already had that character, arising from centuries of handwriting, carving and printing, where the same character drifted into different shapes in different places and for different hands. Both shapes mean the same thing and carry the same reading, and the only decision required was which one to set as the standard for printing. Simplification is a different operation: it takes a character and gives it a new, usually shorter, shape, and the change is made because the old shape was slow to write, not because a second shape had crept in. The distinction matters in practice because the two require different tables. Variants are covered by their own list and a companion list of standard characters with their traditional and variant forms, while simplified forms are covered by the simplification tables. Keeping them apart is what stops a converter from turning a variant into a simplified form, which would silently change a character's shape on a ground that no reform ever intended.
questions.hint: Ask whether the second shape existed before the list was drawn up, and what the list was deciding between.

questions.learningObjective: describe how a lookup code is derived from the four corners of a character
questions.stem: One lookup method gives every character a code of four digits and a fifth digit, built from the shapes found at the four corners of the character, so that a code can be read off the page without knowing the reading. Why was such a system worth building?

options.misconception: treats a shape code as a semantic code, which it is not

options.text: It gave a second way into the dictionary for readers who knew a character's shape but not its reading, which is the usual condition of meeting it in a text
It allowed dictionaries to omit the radical entirely, since four corners classify a character more finely than any component could
options.misconception: overstates the method, since the codes were designed to sit alongside the radical and the stroke count

options.text: It removed the need to know how many strokes a character has, because a code carries that information in its five digits
options.misconception: assumes a code encodes a stroke count, which is not what its digits record

questions.explanation: The four-corner method addresses the situation that actually confronts a reader meeting an unfamiliar character in a text. Such a reader has the shape in front of them and nothing else: not the reading, not the meaning, not the component list, and often not enough English or another language to guess a meaning from. A radical index does not help, because the reader does not know which radical the character would be filed under, and a stroke index helps only if the reader can count the strokes of an unfamiliar shape, which is exactly the skill they may lack. A code read off the four corners needs no such knowledge, since the corners are the parts of a character that are easiest to identify even when the middle is unfamiliar. That is the design insight, and it explains why such systems have been devised and kept in use alongside radical and stroke indexes rather than instead of them. The limits are worth stating too. Codes group characters that resemble each other at the corners, so a code is not unique to one character and the user still has to choose among neighbours, and the codes depend on the printed shape, which is why the same character may be coded differently in different standards.

options.text: The two readings are two ways of pronouncing the same sense, so either one can be used anywhere the character appears
options.misconception: makes the readings interchangeable, which would leave the character with a single sense

The character 乐 is a good example because it was borrowed twice, once in the sense of joy and once in the sense of music, and the two borrowings came in with two different readings, which is why the dictionary lists both and why the two readings carry different tones. The same pattern produced the pairs that surprise learners, where a character has a reading in ordinary words that has nothing to do with its reading in a specialised one, and where the specialist sense survives almost only in fixed terms. The important consequence is for anyone trying to learn the character rather than merely to recognise it. The reading has to be attached to the word, not to the character, because a character with two readings and the character with one are different objects. A learner who attaches a single reading to a character will be wrong in a whole class of words, and the error will not be visible until they meet a word outside the set they practised.

options.text: It marks a pause between clauses, so the notice has been punctuated as two clauses rather than as a list of four items
options.misconception: reads a list separator as a clause boundary, which changes the structure the sentence declares

A space inserted in the wrong place turns a different reading into an unambiguous one, and a space used where a punctuation mark belongs leaves the sentence formally unfinished, since a sentence of this kind is expected to end with a mark. A reader's practical route is therefore a matter of shape familiarity rather than a new language, and it is helped enormously by a conversion tool for the bulk of the text, with the exceptional cases checked by hand. The claim in the fourth option is the trap, since conversion is a table lookup with known exceptions, and treating it as lossless is how silent errors get into a document.

questions.topic: The full stop and the sentence-ending mark
questions.learningObjective: distinguish the Chinese full-width period from a Latin full stop
questions.stem: Chinese text ends a sentence with a small hollow circle placed on the baseline rather than with the solid dot used in English text. What does the difference in shape reflect about the two systems?

options.text: That the circle is a full stop and the dot is an abbreviation mark, so English text cannot be punctuated without the solid dot
options.misconception: misreads a script difference as a difference of function, which reverses the actual relationship

options.text: That the circle marks a question and the dot marks a statement, which is why the two are never mixed in one text
options.misconception: attaches interrogative force to the period, which the system reserves for questions alone

questions.explanation: A writing system that developed its own conventions supplies its own forms for the marks it needs, and the sentence-ending mark is the clearest case. Chinese text closes a sentence with a small hollow circle on the baseline, which is a different mark from the solid dot that closes a sentence in English, and the two are not interchangeable within a line of Chinese text. The reason matters more than the appearance. A reader is expected to read the surrounding marks as belonging to the surrounding script, so a Latin dot dropped into Chinese text reads as a mistake rather than as a variant, and a Chinese circle dropped into English text reads as an intrusion. The same principle runs through the rest of the system, where the question mark, the exclamation mark and the marks of quotation all have forms that are wider than their English counterparts and occupy a full character cell rather than half of one. The practical consequence for anyone producing text is a matter of input settings as much as of knowledge, since a machine that inserts the wrong mark will do so silently in a long document.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: Why a hook is absorbed into its stroke
questions.learningObjective: explain the motor basis of the stroke count in a way that generalises to new characters
questions.stem: Explain why a short hook at the end of a stroke does not add to a character's stroke count, and state the test that would decide the question for a character the reader has never seen before.

answer.exemplar: A good answer builds the argument on pen movement and then shows that the rule is a test rather than a list. The counting unit is a continuous contact between the writing instrument and the surface, from the moment the instrument touches down to the moment it lifts. A stroke may turn, bend, cross itself or finish with a hook while that contact continues, and none of those events breaks the contact, so none of them begins a new stroke. The hook is the clearest case: the writer reaches the end of a vertical and flicks the pen upward in order to leave the stroke cleanly, and the flick is the termination of the movement already in progress rather than a fresh act of writing. This is why the vocabulary of basic strokes is short, since strokes are named for the shape of the main body of the movement and the hook is a property of a stroke's end rather than a stroke of its own. The test that follows is a question about contact and not about appearance. Ask whether the instrument left the surface. If it did not, the movement counts once, however many corners the eye can find. If it did, the next movement counts separately. The test is worth stating in this form because it is decidable from the written character and from the writing conventions, which means it gives an answer for an unfamiliar character rather than a rule that has to be looked up. Its most useful application is diagnostic. A reader who counts a character badly will usually be counting visible corners or visible hooks as separate strokes, and being asked to check the contact at each apparent division removes those extras immediately. The complementary error is the opposite one, merging a genuinely separate movement into a neighbour, and the same test catches it, since a genuine second stroke has to begin after a lift. Applied to the character in the earlier example, the test yields three: a short stroke, a vertical stroke, and one movement that descends, turns along the bottom and hooks upward at the end, with the hook counted inside the third stroke rather than as a fourth.

questions.explanation: The count is a record of movements, and the hook belongs to the movement that ends with it. The temptation in a learner is to read the page rather than the hand, which produces a larger number for every character containing a corner or a flick. Making the test explicit, as this item asks, turns a rule into something a reader can apply to a character they have never met, which is the only version of the rule that is worth having.
questions.hint: Ask what the pen is doing during the hook, and what would count as the beginning of a new stroke.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: Why a radical is not simply a component
questions.learningObjective: distinguish the filing role of a radical from every other role a component plays
questions.stem: A character is built from two components, and a dictionary files it under the left-hand one. Explain what the left-hand component is doing in that character, and why the term for it is not the same as the general word for a part of a character.

answer.exemplar: A good answer separates three jobs that the vocabulary of the language runs together. A character is assembled from components, and one of those components is chosen by a dictionary as the heading under which the character is filed; the term for that chosen component is a radical. The two ideas are not the same, and three differences separate them. First, a character can be assembled from components without any of them being a radical, since a radical is assigned by a classification rather than falling out of the structure. Second, a radical need not be a component of the character at all in the sense of carrying meaning or sound, because it can survive as a filing label after the sound and sense it once contributed have drifted away. Third, the same component can be a radical in one character and an ordinary part in another, so the term is a statement about the indexing, not about the shape. The example in the item makes all three visible. The character is a left-right compound, the reading is fully supplied by the component on the right, and the meaning points to a domain that the left-hand component names rather than to anything the right-hand one contributes. The dictionary files it under the left-hand component because the classification needs a single place to put it, and because the right-hand component is shared with many other characters and would make a useless heading. So the left-hand component is doing real semantic work and is also the filing label, and the reader should be able to say which of those two roles the question is asking about. A useful closing move is to say what would change if the character were filed under the other component: the lookup would succeed for someone who knew that component, would fail for someone who only knew the semantic hint, and the character would move to a different place in the dictionary, which is a different exercise from changing the character's meaning.

questions.explanation: The distinction is a matter of vocabulary, and the item asks for it to be held precisely. A component describes how a character is put together; a radical describes where a dictionary files it. Saying that a radical is a component and nothing more loses the case where a radical carries no meaning, and saying that radicals have nothing to do with components loses the case where a radical is also the semantic hint.
questions.hint: Ask what a component does inside a character, and what a radical does in a dictionary, and then note where the two come apart.

questions.stem: Two reference works give different stroke counts for a set of characters that share one component, and the difference is exactly one for every character in the set. Explain what is being counted differently, and what a reader should do about it.

answer.exemplar: A good answer identifies the shared component as the source of the discrepancy and then refuses to call either count wrong. The set in the question has the pattern that the arithmetic of the difference reveals: a difference of exactly one, for every character, which means the disagreement is not about the individual characters at all but about one component they all carry. That component is the grass component at the top, and the two works are counting the two shapes in which it is written. In the mainland standard the component is written as a single horizontal crossed by two verticals, which is three movements. In the Taiwan standard it is written as two separate crosses, which is four. Every character in the class therefore moves up or down by one depending on the work, and the class is large, several hundred characters, so the discrepancy is systematic rather than a scatter of individual errors. The second part of a good answer says what the difference is not. It is not a difference between simplified and traditional characters, because both sides use a shortened form of this component in simplified writing and both count the same characters; it is a difference in the stroke breakdown of one component, which is a question of shape. The third part is the practical advice, and it should be definite. A count is only ever a count within a convention, so a reader should pick the convention of the material being studied, count by it throughout, and treat a mismatch with a work in the other convention as a difference of standard rather than as an error. The last point is the one that catches people. Because the difference is systematic, a reader who mixes conventions within one list of characters will produce a set that is wrong in a patterned way, and the pattern will be invisible until the list is compared with a table drawn up in the other standard.

The candidate explanations that do not survive are the ones that treat the disagreement character by character, and the explanation that survives is the one that locates it in the single component all of them share.
questions.hint: Ask what a difference of exactly one across every character in a set points to, and then which two shapes of that component are in use.
