questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: What a pinyin input method can and cannot decide
questions.learningObjective: explain the division of labour between a sound-based input method and the writer
questions.stem: A person typing Chinese from a romanised reading gets a list of candidate characters and must choose. Explain what the method is actually doing, and why the choice cannot be taken out of the writer's hands.

answer.exemplar: A good answer describes the direction of travel and then the two kinds of information the writer is the only source of. A method of this kind takes sound and produces characters, which is the reverse of the direction a reader works in. Given a reading, it can say which characters share that reading, and it can order them by how often each is expected, because that is a property of the language rather than of the sentence. What it cannot do is consult the sentence, and the sentence is where the answer lives. The choice between two characters with the same reading is a choice between two meanings, and two meanings are distinguished by what the rest of the sentence is about. A method has no access to that, so it can only offer a ranking, and the ranking is right on average and wrong on any given occasion. Two consequences follow, and a good answer gives both. The first is about learning: since the sound fixes the candidate set but not the member of it, a reading has to be learned together with the words that use it, and a learner who has met a word will recognise it in the list while a learner who has not will not. The second is about the list itself. Because the list is ordered by expected frequency it is a selection rather than a complete inventory, so a character that exists and shares the reading may not appear at all in a short list, and the writer who cannot see it may conclude that it does not exist. The honest summary is that the method removes the typing, not the thinking, and that the state of the surrounding sentence is the only reliable guide to which candidate was meant.

questions.explanation: The method's competence and its blindness are the same fact seen from two sides. It knows the language's frequency statistics, which is why its ordering is well founded, and it has no access to the one place where the intended meaning is recorded, which is why the ordering fails on any particular occasion.
questions.hint: Ask which direction the information flows in, and then ask what the method has not been told about the sentence.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: What a stroke index buys and what it costs
questions.learningObjective: evaluate a lookup method by both what it finds and what it puts in the reader's way
questions.stem: One standard character list is accompanied by a table that orders all of its characters by stroke count alone. Evaluate the table: what does it make possible, and what difficulty does it create?

answer.exemplar: A good answer treats the table as a solution to a real problem that is created by the problem itself, and it names the difficulty without claiming the table is a failure. The problem is the simple characters. A radical classification works by filing a character under one of its components, and that works for the large majority of the language's characters. It cannot work for the characters that do not come apart, and those include some of the most frequent items in the language, so a reader looking for one of them has no heading to search. The stroke index removes the first half of the lookup key altogether. A reader who counts the strokes of an unfamiliar shape and consults the table goes straight to a short run of characters with that count, arranged among characters that are no less unfamiliar, and then narrows by eye. For exactly the class of characters the radical index cannot serve, this is a real improvement, and it is why such a table is published alongside the main list. The difficulty is that counting is the very skill the reader may be missing. Someone who cannot count the strokes of the character in front of them cannot use the table, and someone who counts wrongly lands in the wrong run and may not notice. So the table shifts the difficulty rather than removing it, from a knowledge gap about components to a skill gap about stroke counting. Two further points are worth making. The table depends on the stroke conventions of the standard that compiled it, so the disagreement about component shapes discussed earlier applies here as well, and a table arranged in one convention will misplace characters compiled in the other. And a stroke count is a weak discriminator even when it is right, since the number of characters sharing a count rises with the count, so the crowded bands near the middle of the list are where the reader will spend the most time. The balanced verdict is that the table is a genuine addition for a real gap, that it is not a replacement for the radical index, and that a reader who has both will find the second half of the key the easier one to use.

questions.hint: Ask which characters the radical index cannot serve, and then ask what skill the alternative table demands instead.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: Why a simplified form is a shape and not a sound
questions.learningObjective: explain what a simplification programme does and does not change
questions.stem: Explain why the simplification of written characters is described as a change of shape rather than a change of language, and state which two things a reader of both standards has to relearn.

answer.exemplar: A good answer separates the three layers a written language has, and then says which layer the reform touched. Those layers are the shapes, the sounds and the meanings. The reform worked on the shapes. A long component was replaced by a short one carrying the same sound, which is why the programme is described by reference to strokes and components and never by reference to pronunciation, and why a speaker reading a simplified text aloud is reading the same text. It is worth being explicit about the two things the reform could have changed and did not. It did not change the sounds, so the reading of a character is the same in both standards and a learner who knows the reading of a word knows it in both. It did not change the meanings, so a word means the same thing and a translation carries across unchanged. What a reader of both standards does have to relearn is a pair of shape habits, and they are worth naming separately. The first is a set of new shapes to recognise, several thousand of them, which is an unfamiliarity of appearance and shows up as a failure to identify a character in running text. The second is subtler: because a few simplified forms coincide with forms that already existed, the reader has to decide from context which of two characters is meant, which is a failure of interpretation rather than of recognition. Those two are different problems and they need different remedies, which is why a reader who is told only to learn the new shapes will still be caught out by the second. A final point about scope completes the answer. The reform did not change the writing system, because the system is not a list of shapes but a way of combining components, and the components, the component meanings and the compounding patterns are the same on both sides of the divide.

questions.explanation: The item asks for the layers of a written language to be held apart, since almost every misconception about simplification comes from moving a fact from one layer to another. Once the layers are separate, the questions about readings, meanings and components answer themselves.

Clerical script, the squarer hand with straighter segments that made writing on slips and paper practical
Regular script, the fully settled book hand written one stroke at a time with every character the same size
Running script, which joins neighbouring characters and drops strokes in the interests of speed
Cursive script, which abbreviates far more aggressively and is hard to read without training

questions.explanation: The order is a scale of formality and speed, and each step is defined by what it gives up. Seal script is the starting point because it is the oldest formal hand described, the one of bronze and early stone inscriptions, where the shapes are regular and the proportions are fixed and the writing is slow. Clerical script comes next because it flattened those tall proportions and converted curves into straighter segments, which reduced the number and the precision of the movements the hand had to make and made the script usable on the everyday writing surfaces of the early period. Regular script is the point at which nothing is being saved: every stroke is written separately, every character fills the same square, and the result became the book hand and the model for printing. The last two exist only to go faster. Running script joins neighbouring characters and drops strokes while keeping most shapes recognisable, and cursive script goes much further and is only readable by a trained eye. Two things keep the sequence straight. Regular script belongs in the middle rather than at either end, because it is the slowest of the three later styles and the fastest of the two oldest ones. And clerical script belongs second rather than first, because it is defined by a change made to seal script rather than by anything earlier.
questions.hint: Ask which style is the settled book hand, and then ask which two styles exist in order to save time.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: Finding an unfamiliar character in a dictionary
questions.learningObjective: order the steps of a character lookup from shape to meaning
questions.stem: A reader has met a character in a text and knows nothing about it but its shape. Five steps are listed below in the wrong order. Put them in the order the reader should actually carry them out.

options.text: Decide whether the character can be taken apart at all, since a character that comes apart offers a component to search under
Work out which component of the character, if there is one, is the part a dictionary would file it under
Count the strokes of the character, using the convention of the book being used rather than a different one
Read the entry at the point the two keys have taken you to, and note every reading and every sense the entry lists
Decide which reading and which sense fit the sentence the character was met in, rather than the entry's first line

questions.explanation: The order is dictated by what each step needs from the one before it, which is why it is not as free as it may look. The first step is the branch point, because everything downstream depends on it. A character that comes apart can be filed under a component, and a character that does not has to be found some other way, usually by a stroke count or by a corner code. The second step identifies the heading, and it has to precede the search because a radical index is a directory and a directory is useless without a name to look up. The third step produces the second half of the key, and its place here is also a matter of dependence, since the count orders the characters inside the section the second step has already chosen. The fourth and fifth steps are where the two halves of the job come apart, and the order between them matters more than it may appear. Reading the entry comes first because it supplies the options, and choosing among them comes second because it requires both the entry and the sentence. The fifth step is the one learners most often skip, since the first line of an entry is usually the commonest sense, and taking it without checking is how a reader ends up with a confidently wrong translation of a word they have only just met.
questions.hint: Ask which step decides how the rest of the search is carried out, and which step needs the sentence rather than the book.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: Order of the three parts of a simplified table
questions.learningObjective: order the parts of a simplified character table by the freedom they allow
questions.stem: A table of simplified characters is arranged in three parts, and the arrangement encodes a rule about which forms may be used as components. Five steps are given below in the wrong order. Put them in the order in which a reader applies the table.

options.text: Find the character's heading in the first part, which lists forms that may not be used as components
Check whether the character is in the second part, which lists forms that may be used as components together with a small set of short components
If the character is in neither part, look for it in the third part, where the forms derived from the second part are set out
Check the entry for a reminder note, since a small number of forms carry a note explaining why they are treated as they are
If the character is not listed in any part, apply the general rule that a form derived from a listed component is simplified in the same way

questions.explanation: The three parts of the table are not an alphabetical convenience; they are a rule about how far the simplification may be carried, and consulting them out of order produces the wrong answer. The first part is checked first because it holds the forms that may not be used as components, and a character listed there is settled whatever else the table says. The second part is checked next because it holds the forms that may be used as components, and being in it settles the character and also tells the reader what may be done to other characters containing the same long component. The third part is checked third because it is the largest and it records the results of applying the second part, so a reader consults it after establishing that the character was not settled by the first two. The fourth step is the reminder note, which matters because a small number of forms are not what a mechanical application of the rule would produce, and the notes say why. The fifth step is last because it is the rule of last resort: a character absent from all three lists is still simplified if it contains a listed component, and that is the instruction the table itself gives. A reader who reaches for the general rule first will simplify characters the first part has deliberately excluded, which is the specific error the arrangement was built to prevent.
questions.hint: Ask which part holds the forms that may not be used as components, and which is consulted only after the first two have failed.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: Order of a document's punctuation decisions
questions.learningObjective: sequence the punctuation work on a piece of Chinese text
questions.stem: A writer has drafted a paragraph in Chinese without any punctuation and now has to punctuate it. Five jobs are listed below. Put them in the order that makes the work reliable.

options.text: Decide where the sentences end, since every other mark has to sit inside a sentence or at the end of one
Split each sentence at its internal divisions, choosing between a clause pause and a list separator by what is being held apart
Add the marks for anything enclosed inside a sentence, such as a title, a quotation or an aside
Decide the tone of each sentence and place a question mark, an exclamation mark or a plain full stop accordingly
Read the paragraph aloud from the beginning, checking that the divisions you have marked match how it actually sounds

questions.explanation: The work has a dependency structure, and doing it in the wrong order produces marks that have to be taken out again. Sentence division comes first because it fixes the outer boundaries, and every internal mark has to fall between two of them; a writer who starts by placing pauses has no way to tell whether a pause is a clause division or a boundary between sentences. Internal division comes second, and the choice between the two internal marks is a question about what is being held apart rather than about how long the pause feels. Enclosed material comes third, because an enclosed title or quotation can itself contain a sentence boundary, and marking it before the surrounding sentences are settled gives the wrong scope. Tone comes fourth, since deciding whether a sentence is a question, an exclamation or a statement requires the internal divisions to be in place to be judged at all, and the last mark of a sentence depends on how its middle was marked. The reading pass comes last and is not optional, because punctuation is a set of claims about structure and the only way to test a claim about structure is to see whether the marked-up text still reads as it did unmarked. That final pass catches the two failures that the other steps cannot, which are a sentence boundary placed where the writer only meant a pause and an enclosed quotation whose closing mark has gone missing.
questions.hint: Ask which marks have to sit inside something, and which decision therefore has to be made first.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: A learner who counted a character wrongly
questions.learningObjective: diagnose a stroke-count error and generalise the fix
questions.stem: Stage one: a learner looks a character up in a dictionary, counts its strokes as eight, finds nothing, and counts again as five with no better result. Diagnose what the learner is doing. Stage two: say what the learner should do to get a usable count, and what the learner should do about the two reference works that give different answers.

answer.exemplar: Stage one. The diagnosis has to explain both failures at once, and the commonest explanation does. The learner is reading the page rather than the hand. A count is a record of pen movements, and the eye sees more movements than the hand makes: it sees a corner as a break, and a hook as a separate mark, so the count comes out high, and here it comes out three too high. That is a large error for a count and it is the signature of counting visible features rather than movements. A second possibility has to be checked, because it produces a low count and would explain a different symptom: the learner may be treating the character as an indivisible shape and counting the outline, which loses the strokes of anything in the middle. In this case the error is in the other direction and is too large to be the outline, so the high count is the diagnosis. The reason the learner cannot find the character is that the radical index is ordered by stroke count, and a count of eight lands the reader in a section of characters that have nothing to do with this one. The failure is therefore not a failure of memory or of eyesight; it is a misapplied rule being used as a search key. Stage two. The first correction is to change the test rather than the counting. For every apparent division in the character, ask whether the pen leaves the surface there, and count one stroke for every stretch of continuous contact. Applying that test to this character gives five, since the character is an enclosure written in three movements containing a two-stroke part. The second correction is about the two reference works. A count is only ever a count within a convention, so if two works give different counts for the same character the answer is not that one of them is wrong; it is that the character contains a component whose written shape differs between the two standards, and the counts differ by exactly the number of strokes in that component. The learner's five may be the mainland count and the dictionary's eight the Taiwan count, or the reverse, and the way to find out which is to look at what the character has at the top. The habit to leave the learner with is to pick the convention of the book being used and count by it throughout, and to treat a mismatch with the other convention as a difference of standard rather than as an error to be corrected.

questions.explanation: The item is diagnostic, and the mark of a good answer is that it names the specific counting error and then generalises the correction into a test the learner can apply to a character they have never seen. A diagnosis that only says the count is wrong leaves the learner where they were.
questions.hint: Ask whether the error is high or low, since that distinguishes counting visible corners from counting only the outline.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: A conversion that changed the wrong sense
questions.learningObjective: diagnose a silent error in automatic text conversion
questions.stem: Stage one: an older document has been run through a simplified-to-traditional converter, and one sentence now says that an empress lives at a place where it used to say that somebody worked there. Diagnose the fault. Stage two: say what the converter should have consulted, and what a reader has to do to the rest of the document.

answer.exemplar: Stage one. The fault is a correspondence that the converter treated as one to one where it is one to many, and the reason it is silent is that the output is a real character. The simplified form standing for the traditional character meaning after or later is also the simplified form of a different traditional character, one meaning an empress or a queen, which was already a character in its own right with that meaning. A converter that holds a table of pairs reads the form, finds one traditional character to put in its place, and writes it in. On the instances where that is the right answer the output is correct, and on the instances where it is the wrong answer the output is still a well-formed character in a sentence that still parses. Nothing in the document shows an error, which is exactly what makes this class of failure dangerous. The symptom here is a sentence whose sense has changed category, from a claim about a person's career to a claim about a royal residence, and the diagnosis is confirmed by asking which two traditional characters share the simplified form in the table. Stage two. The converter should have consulted a list of the exceptions before applying the general table, because the general table is built on component substitution and cannot represent a case where one form stands for two characters. The official comparison of standard characters with traditional and variant forms does exactly this, setting the non-corresponding cases out separately, and a converter that ignores that list will fail on every one of them. For the reader, the consequence is a limit on what the conversion can be trusted for. The bulk of the text can be taken as reliable enough to work from, because the general correspondences hold almost everywhere, and the exception list is short enough to be handled. The remaining obligation is to read the converted text for the known exception forms, and to check any sentence in which those forms occur, since those are the only places an error can hide. A converted document that has been read in this way is a usable document; one that has been trusted wholesale is a document whose errors are invisible.

questions.explanation: The item asks for a diagnosis and then for the cure, and a good answer notes that the error is silent because the output is a well-formed character. Recognising that silence is the feature of the fault is what tells a reader where to look in the rest of the text.
questions.hint: Ask how many traditional characters share the simplified form that was converted, and what a table of simple pairs can do with that number.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: A headline whose shortened form changes the reading
questions.learningObjective: assess the risk of a shortened form in a short text with no context
questions.stem: Stage one: a headline in the simplified forms uses a word that could stand for two different characters, and the surrounding words do not rule either out. Say what the reader faces. Stage two: say which register the risk belongs to, and what a writer should do about it.

answer.exemplar: Stage one. The reader faces an ambiguity that would be harmless in a longer text and is serious in a headline, and the reason is the amount of context available. A handful of simplified forms coincide with forms that already existed with an unrelated meaning, so a word containing one of them can be two different words. In a paragraph the surrounding sentences would almost always settle it, because the next clause is about a person's job or a period of time and the other reading would be about a royal figure, and the fit is decisive. A headline has no such next clause. It is a fragment, it is written to be read in a line or two, and often it is read alone in a list of other headlines, so the reader has a few words at most. The result is that the two readings are both live, and a reader who takes the more frequent one without noticing may carry a wrong sense out of the headline and into a conversation about it. The difficulty is not that the character is obscure; it is that the text is short. Stage two. The risk belongs to the written registers rather than to speech, and that distinction is worth making precisely. Spoken language supplies what the headline lacks. A speaker says the word inside a sentence, the tone and the surrounding words resolve the ambiguity, and the listener's ear does half the work before the vocabulary is consulted. Written registers differ in how much context they carry, and a headline carries the least, which puts it at the opposite end from a conversation. A writer's options are three and they should be chosen deliberately. Replace the word with one that has only the intended reading. Add the missing words, restoring the context that resolves it, at the cost of a slightly longer headline. Or keep the word and accept that a share of readers will take the other reading, which is a defensible choice for a headline about a person where both readings are amusing but not for a headline making a factual claim. What a writer should not do is assume that the ambiguity is resolved by the reader's care, because a careful reader with no context is in exactly the same position as a careless one.

questions.explanation: The item asks for an assessment of a risk rather than a rule, and the useful part of the answer is the observation that the difficulty comes from the length of the text rather than from the obscurity of the character. That reframes the problem from vocabulary to register.
questions.hint: Ask how much context a headline gives a reader, and then ask what a speaker has that a headline writer does not.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: A text that mixes two regional standards
questions.learningObjective: assess the readability of a text that mixes two approved forms
questions.stem: Stage one: a document has been edited so that some characters appear in the simplified forms and others in the traditional ones, without anyone intending to make a political point. Say what a reader faces. Stage two: say whether a reader can rely on the shape to tell which sense was meant anywhere in such a text.

answer.exemplar: Stage one. The reader faces a text whose reliability can no longer be judged from its appearance, and that is a worse position than either consistent standard. In a document written wholly in one standard, a reader who knows the other standard can convert it with a table and know that the exceptions are few and checkable. In a mixed document the conversion table no longer describes the text, because the document no longer corresponds to any single list. A reader who applies the table will produce a text in which every character has been changed, including the ones that were already correct, and will have no way to tell which of those changes were necessary. The result is a document that looks tidied and is in fact less trustworthy than the original, since the original at least stated its own standard and the tidied one does not. There is a second cost, which is to the eye. Chinese readers read the shapes as well as the words, and a text that switches shape on the same character or the same family of characters reads as careless even when the sense is perfectly clear, because the inconsistency itself carries a signal and the signal here is that nobody decided. Stage two. The answer has to be that shape can no longer be trusted as evidence anywhere in the text, and the reason is worth stating precisely. Shape was already never a guarantee, since a few simplified forms correspond to more than one traditional character, and in a consistent text the reader could at least reason from the standard the text follows. In a mixed text the reader cannot even do that, because there is no standard to reason from. The only sound procedure is to stop using shape as evidence and go to the language. A reader should read the text for meaning, treating any decision about which character was intended as a question about the sentence rather than about the printing, and should assume that the ambiguity is no longer resolvable by inspection. A writer who finds a mixed document has two honest options, which are to convert the whole of it to one standard using a table and then check the exception forms, or to restore the original text and leave the standard as it was. What cannot be recommended is a partial conversion, because that is the state the document is already in and it is the state that has just been described as the problem.

questions.explanation: The item asks for an assessment of a mixed text, and the mark of a good answer is that it explains why the mixed state is worse than either pure one. The comparison is the point: a reader with a table is well served by a consistent document and badly served by an inconsistent one.
questions.hint: Ask what a conversion table assumes about the text it is applied to, and then ask whether a mixed text satisfies that assumption.
